title: Advanced Conditional Access and risk-based policies
summary: Design layered Conditional Access policies that combine identity, device and risk signals, then enforce them with authentication strengths, session controls and Identity Protection risk-based policies. You will roll changes out safely with report-only mode and protect break-glass accounts from lockout.
objectives: Break a Conditional Access policy into its assignments and access controls and explain what each lever does
Design a layered set of policies rather than one monolithic rule, and reason about policy intersection
Distinguish sign-in risk from user risk and map each to the correct Identity Protection policy
Require phishing-resistant authentication using authentication strengths instead of the legacy MFA toggle
Apply session controls — sign-in frequency, persistent browser, app-enforced restrictions and CAE
Roll policies out safely with report-only mode and exclude break-glass emergency access accounts

quiz.q: A Conditional Access policy is structured as assignments and access controls. Which item is an ASSIGNMENT rather than an access control?
options: Require device to be marked as compliant
quiz.why: Assignments define WHO and WHAT a policy targets — users/groups, target resources, and conditions. Grant requirements like MFA, compliant device or app protection policy are access controls that fire once the assignment matches.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between sign-in risk and user risk in Microsoft Entra Identity Protection?
options: Sign-in risk is about the account being compromised over time; user risk is about a single authentication
Sign-in risk reflects the probability that a specific authentication is not the legitimate owner; user risk reflects the probability the account itself is compromised
They are identical and used interchangeably
User risk only applies to guest accounts
quiz.why: Sign-in risk is real-time and per-authentication (impossible travel, anonymous IP, unfamiliar properties), so the right remediation is MFA. User risk is a cumulative judgement that the identity is compromised (leaked credentials, confirmed-compromise patterns), so the right remediation is a secure password change.

quiz.q: You want to require phishing-resistant authentication for admins. What is the correct modern mechanism?
options: The legacy 'Require multifactor authentication' grant control
An authentication strength that allows only phishing-resistant methods (FIDO2, Windows Hello for Business, certificate-based)
Enabling the per-user MFA toggle in the legacy portal
quiz.why: Authentication strengths let you require a specific set of methods. The built-in phishing-resistant strength permits only FIDO2 security keys, Windows Hello for Business and certificate-based authentication — stronger and more precise than the generic MFA grant.

quiz.q: Which session control causes the browser session to be re-evaluated and revoked in near real time when critical events occur, rather than waiting for token expiry?
quiz.why: Continuous access evaluation lets resource providers honour near-real-time revocation events (account disable, password reset, elevated risk). Sign-in frequency forces periodic reauthentication but is not real-time; persistent browser and app-enforced restrictions serve different purposes.

quiz.q: Explain why break-glass (emergency access) accounts must be excluded from Conditional Access policies, and one safeguard you apply instead.
quiz.answer: A misconfigured or dependency-broken policy (for example one requiring a compliant device, a specific MFA provider, or a location you cannot reach) can lock every admin out of the tenant. Two cloud-only break-glass accounts excluded from all policies guarantee you can still sign in to fix it. Safeguards include long random passphrases, phishing-resistant MFA where possible, tight sign-in alerting/monitoring, and periodic credential testing.
quiz.why: Excluding break-glass accounts prevents a single bad policy or a downed MFA/identity dependency from permanently locking administrators out, while monitoring and strong credentials limit the risk those highly privileged exclusions create.

quiz.q: In one or two sentences, describe how report-only mode supports a safe Conditional Access rollout and what you inspect before enabling.
quiz.answer: Report-only mode evaluates the policy against real sign-ins and records what WOULD have happened without actually enforcing grant or block, so you can detect unintended impact. You inspect the sign-in logs and the Conditional Access Insights workbook to see which users, apps and sessions would have been affected, confirm break-glass accounts are excluded, then flip to On.
quiz.why: Report-only surfaces the real-world blast radius — including surprises like service accounts or legacy clients — before enforcement, which is the safest way to avoid mass lockouts when a new policy goes live.

body_markdown:
## Anatomy of a Conditional Access policy

Every Conditional Access policy is an if-then statement: **if** these assignments match, **then** apply these access controls. Master the anatomy and the rest follows.

- **Assignments** define the scope. They are **users** (or workload identities), **target resources** (cloud apps, user actions like registering security info, or authentication context), and **conditions** (sign-in risk, user risk, device platform, locations, client apps, device filters).
- **Access controls** define the outcome. **Grant** controls either block or grant with requirements such as **require MFA**, **require compliant device**, **require Intune-managed or hybrid-joined device**, **require app protection policy**, or **require authentication strength**. **Session** controls shape the resulting session.

A policy with no matching assignment never fires. A policy that matches always applies its controls — and **multiple matching policies combine**: all grant requirements are ANDed together, and any single block wins.

## Design layered, not monolithic

Resist the urge to cram everything into one rule. Build small, single-purpose policies so intersection is predictable and troubleshooting is sane:

```text
CA001  Block legacy authentication            (all users)
CA002  Require phishing-resistant MFA          (admin roles)
CA003  Require compliant device                (all users, M365 apps)
CA004  Require MFA on sign-in risk = medium+   (all users)
CA005  Require password change on user risk    (all users)
CA006  Sign-in frequency 12h + no persistence  (unmanaged devices)
CA000  EXCLUDE break-glass accounts            (every policy)
```

Each policy does one thing. Together they form a defence-in-depth mesh where the grant requirements stack.

## Sign-in risk versus user risk

**Identity Protection** produces two distinct risk signals and they need different remediation.

- **Sign-in risk** is the probability that a *single authentication* is not the legitimate owner — impossible travel, anonymous IP, unfamiliar properties. Remediate in real time by **requiring MFA**.
- **User risk** is the cumulative probability that the *account itself* is compromised — leaked credentials, confirmed-compromise patterns. Remediate by **requiring a secure password change** (self-service password reset with MFA), which also dismisses the risk.

You wire these in as conditions on Conditional Access grant controls:

```json
{
  "conditions": { "signInRiskLevels": ["high", "medium"] },
  "grantControls": {
    "operator": "OR",
    "builtInControls": ["mfa"]
  }
}
```

## Strengths, session controls and locations

Drop the legacy MFA toggle for privileged access. An **authentication strength** lets you demand specific methods; the built-in **phishing-resistant** strength permits only **FIDO2**, **Windows Hello for Business** and **certificate-based** authentication.

**Session controls** govern the session after grant: **sign-in frequency** forces periodic reauthentication; **persistent browser** controls staying signed in; **app-enforced restrictions** let Office and SharePoint limit downloads on unmanaged devices; and **continuous access evaluation (CAE)** revokes sessions in near real time on critical events. **Named locations** and **device filters** sharpen conditions — for example, treating a trusted country differently or excluding a kiosk by its device attributes.

Find risky sign-ins to validate your risk policies:

```kql
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RiskLevelDuringSignIn in ("high", "medium")
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName,
          RiskLevelDuringSignIn, ConditionalAccessStatus, IPAddress
| order by TimeGenerated desc
```

## Roll out safely and avoid lockout

Never flip a new policy straight to On. Set it to **report-only**, let it observe real sign-ins, and read the **Conditional Access Insights** workbook and sign-in logs to see who *would* have been blocked. Surprises — service accounts, legacy clients, a forgotten region — show up here, not in a flood of help-desk tickets.

The non-negotiable safeguard: maintain two cloud-only **break-glass** accounts **excluded from every policy**, with long random passphrases, monitored sign-in alerts, and periodic testing. A policy that requires a compliant device or a downed MFA provider can otherwise lock out every admin — break-glass is your way back in.

## Your task

In a test tenant, design and document a layered set of at least five Conditional Access policies covering: block legacy auth, phishing-resistant strength for admins, compliant-device requirement, a sign-in-risk MFA policy and a user-risk password-change policy. Create each in **report-only** mode, confirm both break-glass accounts are excluded from all of them, run the Insights workbook for 48 hours, and write up the would-be impact (affected users, apps, sessions) plus any misconfiguration you caught before enabling enforcement.

slides.title: Advanced Conditional Access and risk-based policies
slides.sub: Month 3 - Advanced Endpoint Security & Identity  |  Lesson 2
slides.narration: Welcome back to Month Three. In the last lesson we set the Zero Trust mindset; now we build the engine that enforces it: Conditional Access. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to break a policy into its parts, design layered policies instead of one giant rule, wire in risk-based remediation, demand phishing-resistant authentication, shape sessions, and roll the whole thing out without locking anyone out.

slides.title: Anatomy of a policy
bullets: A policy is an if-then: if assignments match, then apply controls.
Assignments: users, target resources, and conditions.
Access controls: grant controls and session controls.
No match means it never fires; a match always applies.
slides.narration: At its core, every Conditional Access policy is an if-then statement. If these assignments match, then apply these access controls. The assignments are the scope: which users, which target resources like cloud apps or user actions, and which conditions. The access controls are the outcome: grant controls that block or require something, and session controls that shape the session. If nothing matches, the policy does nothing. If it matches, it always applies.

slides.title: Grant controls stack
bullets: Grant controls: block, or grant with requirements.
Require M F A, compliant device, app protection, strength.
Multiple matching policies AND their requirements together.
Any single block wins over every grant.
slides.narration: Let's zoom in on grant controls. A policy either blocks, or grants access subject to requirements: require M F A, require a compliant device, require an app protection policy, or require an authentication strength. The important subtlety is how policies combine. When several policies match the same sign-in, all of their grant requirements are AND-ed together. And if any one policy says block, block wins. That combining behaviour is exactly why we design small policies.

slides.title: Design layered, not monolithic
bullets: Build small, single-purpose policies.
Predictable intersection, far easier troubleshooting.
One policy blocks legacy auth, another requires strength.
Together they form defence in depth.
slides.code:
CA001 Block legacy authentication      (all users)
CA002 Require phishing-resistant MFA    (admins)
CA003 Require compliant device          (all, M365)
CA004 MFA on sign-in risk medium+       (all users)
CA005 Password change on user risk      (all users)
CA000 EXCLUDE break-glass accounts      (every policy)
slides.narration: Please resist the temptation to cram everything into one mega-policy. Build small, single-purpose policies, each doing exactly one thing. Here's a typical set: one blocks legacy authentication, one requires phishing-resistant M F A for admins, one requires a compliant device, one handles sign-in risk, one handles user risk. Because each is focused, their intersection is predictable and troubleshooting stays sane. And notice the last line, present on every single policy: exclude the break-glass accounts.

slides.title: Sign-in risk vs user risk
bullets: Sign-in risk: is this one authentication legitimate?
Remediate sign-in risk in real time with M F A.
User risk: is the account itself compromised?
Remediate user risk with a secure password change.
slides.narration: Identity Protection gives you two different risk signals, and they need different fixes. Sign-in risk asks: is this single authentication really the legitimate owner? Think impossible travel or an anonymous I P. The right remediation is real-time, so require M F A. User risk is different: it's the cumulative judgement that the account itself is compromised, for example through leaked credentials. There, requiring M F A isn't enough; you require a secure password change, which also clears the risk.

slides.title: Risk-based policies in practice
bullets: Identity Protection feeds risk into Conditional Access.
Set sign-in risk levels as a condition, grant requires M F A.
User-risk policy requires password change via S S P R.
Tune thresholds: high only, or medium and high.
slides.narration: Here's how that looks in a policy. Identity Protection calculates the risk, and Conditional Access consumes it as a condition. In this snippet we match sign-in risk of high or medium, and the grant control requires M F A. For the user-risk equivalent, you'd match user risk levels and require a password change through self-service password reset. Start cautious. Many teams begin enforcing on high only, watch the results, then extend to medium once they trust the signal.

slides.title: Authentication strengths
bullets: Retire the legacy 'require M F A' toggle for admins.
An authentication strength demands specific methods.
Phishing-resistant: FIDO2, Windows Hello, certificates.
Apply it to privileged roles and sensitive apps.
slides.narration: For privileged access, the generic require-M-F-A control is too blunt — not all M F A is equal, and push-based factors can be phished. Authentication strengths let you demand specific methods. The built-in phishing-resistant strength permits only F I D O 2 security keys, Windows Hello for Business, and certificate-based authentication. Apply that strength to your admin roles and your most sensitive apps, and you've raised the bar from any second factor to factors that genuinely resist phishing.

slides.title: Session controls and locations
bullets: Sign-in frequency forces periodic reauthentication.
Persistent browser and app-enforced restrictions limit risk.
C A E revokes sessions in near real time on key events.
Named locations and device filters sharpen conditions.
slides.code:
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RiskLevelDuringSignIn in ("high","medium")
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName,
          AppDisplayName, ConditionalAccessStatus, IPAddress
slides.narration: After access is granted, session controls shape what that session looks like. Sign-in frequency forces reauthentication on a schedule. Persistent browser controls whether users stay signed in. App-enforced restrictions let Office and SharePoint block downloads on unmanaged devices. And continuous access evaluation, C A E, revokes sessions in near real time when something critical happens. Named locations and device filters let you sharpen conditions. This K Q L query pulls risky sign-ins so you can validate your risk policies against reality.

slides.title: Safe rollout and break-glass
bullets: Never flip straight to On — use report-only first.
Read the Insights workbook and sign-in logs for impact.
Keep two cloud-only break-glass accounts.
Exclude them from every policy; monitor and test them.
slides.narration: Rolling out is where careers are made or broken. Never flip a new policy straight to On. Set it to report-only, let it watch real sign-ins, then read the Conditional Access Insights workbook and the sign-in logs to see who would have been blocked. Service accounts and legacy clients will surprise you here, safely. And the non-negotiable: keep two cloud-only break-glass accounts, excluded from every policy, with long passphrases, monitored alerts and periodic testing. They are your way back in if a policy locks everyone out.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Assignments scope it; grant and session controls enforce it.
Sign-in risk wants M F A; user risk wants a password change.
Phishing-resistant strength plus session controls and C A E.
Task: design 5+ layered policies in report-only, document impact.
slides.narration: Let's recap. A policy is assignments plus access controls; design small layered policies so they stack predictably. Sign-in risk is remediated with M F A, user risk with a secure password change. Use authentication strengths for phishing-resistant M F A, and session controls plus C A E to govern the session continuously. Your task: in a test tenant, design at least five layered policies — block legacy auth, phishing-resistant strength for admins, compliant device, sign-in-risk M F A, and user-risk password change. Create them all in report-only, confirm both break-glass accounts are excluded, run the Insights workbook for forty-eight hours, and write up the would-be impact and any misconfiguration you caught. See you in the next lesson.
